title: Breaking an oath
hook: the expiation for a broken oath is feeding ten poor people (5:89)

segments.voice: Yesterday: compete in good. Your line was race in good. Did you get ahead of someone in kindness without telling them? Today, what happens when a promise sworn by God goes wrong. Day three hundred ninety-five.

Wallahi. By God. In much of the Muslim world it's the most common word in an argument about who ate the last samosa. Wallahi I didn't. Wallahi I'll be there in five minutes. It slips out so easily it barely registers. And then there's the other kind: the oath sworn in earnest, in anger. By God, I will never speak to you again. What does the Qur'an do with a person who swore something like that and now wishes they hadn't? It doesn't shrug. It doesn't trap them either. It hands them a bill, payable to the hungry.
screen: `WALLAHI — BY GOD.` → `NEVER SPEAKING TO YOU AGAIN.` → `A BILL, PAYABLE TO THE HUNGRY.`

segments.voice: Surah five, verse eighty-nine, draws a line between two kinds of oath. The first is laghw, idle talk: the oaths that fall out of your mouth without meaning to bind anything. Allah, the verse says, doesn't take you to task for those. A report in Bukhari has Aishah explaining them as the everyday no, by God, and yes, by God, of casual speech. The second kind is the oath sworn deliberately. Break that one, and there's a cost. In Pickthall's words: “The expiation thereof is the feeding of ten of the needy,” with the average of what you feed your own family. Or clothing ten people. Or freeing a slave, which in the Qur'an's world was one of its repeated ways of draining slavery away. And if none of that is possible, three days of fasting. The word is kaffarah. Its root, k-f-r, means to cover over. A farmer covers seed with soil. A kaffarah covers a broken word, not by pretending it wasn't broken, but by laying something good on top of it. And there's a twist. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim says that if someone swears to do something, then sees that something else is better, they should do the better thing and pay the expiation. So the oath to never speak to your brother isn't a cage. Break it, feed ten people, and go call him. The verse closes by telling believers to guard their oaths. The simplest way to guard them is to swear fewer of them.
screen: `LAGHW — THE OATHS THAT SLIP OUT.` · `TEN OF THE NEEDY, FED.` · `K-F-R — TO COVER OVER.` · `DO THE BETTER THING, AND PAY.` · then, large: `SWEAR LESS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Think back over the last week: where did you swear something, or promise something big, more than you needed to? By God. I swear. I'll never. Notice how often the big words were standing in for a plain yes or no. Then think of one person you could feed today: a friend, a coworker, someone on the street, a food bank donation. Let the two thoughts sit together until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Kaffarah. Expiation: the covering of a broken oath, by feeding ten people, clothing them, freeing someone, or fasting three days. Today's word.
Your line: swear less. Today, say a plain yes or no where you'd usually reach for a big word. And feed someone. Day three hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Muslims who break a deliberate oath pay kaffarah, most often by feeding ten needy people or giving the equivalent through a mosque or charity; if they can't, they fast three days. Many teachers also discourage swearing by God in everyday talk.

original.note: Arabic: expiation, from k-f-r, to cover over.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fine for breaking a promise.
what it means: a way to cover a broken oath with good: feeding, clothing, freeing, or fasting.
what a scholar hears: jurists distinguish laghw (idle), deliberate oaths, and false oaths about the past, which most say kaffarah does not cover; that last one calls for repentance.
